How to perform a basic clinical screen (supine fingertip test)
1. Position:
   - Lie on back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor, pelvis neutral (not strongly tucked). Head supported with a small pillow if needed.
2. Hand placement:
   - Place fingers of one hand in a vertical line along the midline of the abdomen (index, middle, ring fingers stacked) with fingertips across the linea alba.
   - Check at three levels: just above the belly button (about 2 cm), at the level of the belly button, and just below the belly button (2–3 cm below). You can also check higher (just under the ribs) if needed.
3. The test movement:
   - Ask her to take a slow diaphragmatic inhale, then exhale and gently tilt the pelvis (posterior pelvic tilt) to flatten the low back and perform a small head lift or curl-up (lift head/shoulders just enough to feel the abdominal contraction) — stop if she feels bulging or doming.
   - While she holds that small lift (or during the lift), press gently downward with the fingers to perceive the width and depth of the gap.
4. How to measure/interpret:
   - Width (finger count): Note how many finger widths fit in the midline gap.
     - 0–1 fingers = likely normal
     - 2+ fingers may indicate separation (diastasis) — more caution advised
   - Depth (tissue thickness): If you can feel a deep gap (fingers sink in and you feel little connective tissue resistance), that suggests a larger separation or thin linea alba — be more conservative.
   - Quality of contraction: Watch and feel for coning or doming (a ridge forming down the midline) when she lifts. Coning/doming = sign of poor load transfer and reason to regress.

Notes and caveats
- Finger-width cutoffs are approximate; reliable assessment uses calipers/ultrasound and clinician training. This finger test is a practical screening tool to guide progression, not a definitive diagnosis.
- Avoid maximal sit-ups — use only a small head‑lift/curl and breathing to assess.
- Women who are postpartum and breastfeeding may have more laxity temporarily — interpret results alongside symptoms.

What to do based on screening results (progression rules)
- If 0–1 finger width and no doming/heaviness:
  - Proceed with planned progressions but continue monitoring. Emphasize anti‑flexion core drills and breath/pelvic‑floor coordination.
- If 2 fingers or more OR any doming/coning OR tissue feels very thin:
  - Treat as clinically significant diastasis: regress to lower challenge levels.
  - Avoid loaded spinal flexion, heavy carries without pelvic floor coordination, and longer valsalva efforts.
  - Focus 1–2 weeks on deep core/pelvic floor retraining (dead bugs with small range, pallof holds, supine breathing, heel slides, glute bridges), reduce external load, shorten lever length, and re-test after 1–2 weeks.
  - Consider referral to pelvic‑health physiotherapist for formal assessment and individualized rehabilitation.
- If any pelvic heaviness/prolapse symptoms, new or worsening urinary incontinence, or pain:
  - Stop progression, regress exercise intensity/volume, and refer to pelvic‑health physio/OB.

Ongoing checks during sessions
- Watch for visible bulging/coning during:
  - Heel slides
  - Dead bugs
  - Planks
  - Any loaded anti‑flexion movement (pallof, carries, overhead press)
- Ask after cardio/longer sessions if she feels pelvic heaviness; increase rest and regress if present.

Coaching cues during testing and training to reduce false positives
- Ensure neutral pelvis and no breath‑holding during the test.
- Ask her to perform a gentle pelvic floor lift + slight drawing in on exhale; avoid a hard Valsalva.
- If doming occurs with a strong contraction, that suggests poor coordination rather than absence of core function — emphasize retraining.

Documentation and referral thresholds
- Document finger width, tissue feel (thick vs thin), presence/absence of doming, and symptoms after test.
- Refer to pelvic‑health physiotherapist if:
  - Gap ≥2 finger widths with thin tissue or persistent doming
  - Any pelvic organ prolapse symptoms (heaviness, pressure, bulge)
  - Any persistent urinary/fecal incontinence worsening
  - Uncertainty about testing or poor progress after conservative retraining

Good goal — a 10K in the autumn is realistic if we progress cautiously and hit a few key pelvic‑health and strength milestones first. Returning to running postpartum is less about a fixed number of weeks and more about meeting functional criteria and building a graded return that protects the pelvic floor and abdominal wall.

Summary timeline (typical)
- Earliest safe reintroduction of running: not before cleared for impact (your OB said no jumping for ~4 more weeks). Realistically plan earliest running trials around 14–16 weeks postpartum, but only if screening and functional criteria are met.
- A safer, conservative pathway is to begin walk‑run reintroduction around 12–16 weeks postpartum only when pelvic floor/core checks pass and strength/base conditioning are solid. Full training for a 10K may take 8–12 weeks of progressive running work after initial run tolerance is established.

Prerequisites before any running trials
1) Medical clearance: explicit OB clearance for impact activities (running). If the OB gave only “no jumping for 4 weeks” ensure you re-check before starting running.
2) Diastasis and pelvic‑floor screening:
   - Supine fingertip test: gap ≤1 finger at/around the umbilicus, tissue reasonably thick, and no doming/coning during cough/head lift/heavy core work.
   - No pelvic heaviness, bulging, or increased/new urinary leakage with current training and after cardio/HIIT sessions for at least 2 weeks.
   - If any symptoms or gap ≥2 fingers, refer to pelvic‑health physio and delay running progression.
3) Strength & control milestones (functional criteria, not just time):
   - Consistent ability to perform anti‑flexion core work without coning: long‑lever dead bug, Pallof press (30–40s each side), 30–60s plank (knee or full depending on baseline) with good breathing and no doming.
   - Lower‑body strength: comfortable with single‑leg movements (split squat/Bulgarian split, single‑leg RDL) with controlled 8–12 reps and minimal fatigue.
   - Loaded carries: carry/hold heavier loads for 45–60s with neutral core (farmer/suitcase carries).
   - Tolerance to higher‑intensity low‑impact cardio (e.g., 4–6 × 3–4 min bike intervals at RPE 6–7) with no pelvic symptoms for 2+ weeks.
4) Recovery & general readiness:
   - Sleep, nutrition/hydration adequate; breastfeeding considerations (time feedings before runs).
   - No persistent pelvic pain or urinary/fecal incontinence worsening.

A graded running return plan (example to start once prerequisites are met)
Phase 0 — Pre‑run conditioning (2 weeks minimum)
- Continue strength program (2–3/week) and low-impact cardio/HIIT.
- Build up impact tolerance with brisk walks, progressing to 30–60 min walks and short faster walking intervals and low‑impact faster cycling.
- Include 1–2 sessions/week of run‑prep: progressive single‑leg work, reactive hops off a step (only when cleared for impact and pelvic floor ok) — otherwise use step‑ups and fast marching.

Phase 1 — Walk‑run reintroduction (2 weeks)
- Session example (3 sessions/week, non-consecutive):
  - Warm-up 8–10 min brisk walk + dynamic mobility + breathing
  - Work: 6–8 repeats of 1 min easy run / 2 min brisk walk (total hard time 6–8 min). Keep run pace conversational, RPE 5–6.
  - Cool-down 5–10 min walk + diaphragmatic breathing and pelvic-floor reset.
- Progression: increase run interval length (1 → 2 → 3 min) or decrease recovery only if no pelvic symptoms for 1 week between increases.

Phase 2 — Gradual mileage build (4–6 weeks)
- 3 run sessions per week:
  - 1 easy continuous run (start 10–15 min easy, build 5–10 min per week up to 30–40 min).
  - 1 interval/tempo session (short intervals like 6 × 2–3 min at moderate effort with ample recovery).
  - 1 long walk/run (steady walk with run segments or continuous easy run building time).
- Increase overall weekly running volume by no more than ~10–15% per week.
- Continue strength 1–2× per week (maintain pelvic‑floor focus). Strength helps protect against injury and supports pelvic floor.
- Monitor symptoms closely after each run and in the 24–48 hours after.

Phase 3 — Specific 10K training (6–8 weeks)
- After comfortable 3–4 weeks of continuous running (e.g., 3 runs/week, longest 30–45 min) with no symptoms, you can progress to a structured 8–10 week 10K plan (mix of easy runs, a quality session per week, and a long run).
- Keep total weekly running increases conservative and keep at least one strength session per week that includes anti‑flexion core and hip control.

Key coaching cues and pelvic‑floor management when running
- Breathing: avoid breath‑holding. Establish a breathing rhythm (inhale 2–3 steps, exhale 2–3 steps) that keeps exhalation active on harder efforts.
- Pelvic‑floor cue: gentle lift and co‑contraction on exhale; avoid forceful bearing down during strides.
- Posture: maintain upright torso, avoid excessive forward flexion; shorter cadence (higher cadence ~170–180 steps/min may reduce impact per step) can sometimes reduce pelvic load — gradually experiment to find comfortable cadence.
- Footstrike & cadence: softer, midfoot strike and slightly increased cadence reduce impact loading; coach gradual changes only.
- Footwear: use supportive running shoes and consider cushioned surfaces (track, treadmill, softer trails) initially rather than hard concrete.

Monitoring and red flags (stop running and regress to walking/conditioning)
- New or increased pelvic heaviness or pressure (either during or after run)
- Visible bulging/coning at the abdomen during or after run
- New or increased urinary/fecal leakage
- Sharp pelvic/abdominal pain
- If any occur, reduce to walking and low‑impact cardio immediately and refer to pelvic‑health physiotherapist.

Practical timeline example for an autumn 10K (today = ~10 weeks postpartum; autumn say 20–24 weeks away)
- If autumn is ~12–16 weeks away, you have time to progress:
  - Weeks 10–14: complete the on‑ramp (strength + HIIT + low‑impact cardio) and aim for pelvic‑floor/diastasis checks by week 14.
  - Weeks 14–16: start walk‑run reintroduction if cleared and criteria met.
  - Weeks 16–20+: gradually build to continuous runs and a 6–8 week 10K training block so she’s ready by autumn.
- If autumn is sooner (<10 weeks away), be more conservative: prioritize safety and consider setting the 10K as a late-autumn goal if needed.

Practical tips for training and life
- Schedule runs when she’s most likely to have energy and after feeding/pumping to avoid discomfort.
- Use short run segments if time/energy are limited. Consistency matters more than single long efforts early on.
- Keep a simple symptom log after each run (pelvic heaviness Y/N, leakage Y/N, doming Y/N).
- If at any point you are unsure, get a pelvic‑health physiotherapist involved for tailored clearance and progression.

- Produce a printable run‑return checklist and symptom log for you and the client.

Here’s a concise week-by-week summary of the 4-week postpartum on‑ramp (10 weeks postpartum, OB cleared for moderate exercise, no jumping 4 more weeks). Includes what each week looks like and the screening checkpoints.

Overview (weekly structure)
- Frequency: 3 strength sessions/week (full-body + anti‑flexion core + mobility). Optional 1–2 low-impact cardio sessions/week. Add 1 low‑impact HIIT session/week once screened and tolerated (mid‑Week 2+). Daily 2–5 min breathing/pelvic‑floor micro sessions.
- Equipment: light dumbbells, mat, chair, optional band, stationary bike or step for cardio.
- Intensity progression: Week 1 = acclimatisation (RPE ~4–5). Weeks 2–4 = gradual increase to RPE ~6–7. Avoid impact/jumping throughout.

Week 1 — Acclimatisation
- Goal: reconnect breathing & pelvic floor, assess baseline movement quality, low volume and light loads.
- Sessions (3): short warm-up, breathing + pelvic-floor activation, basic strength (goblet squat to chair, rows, glute bridges, gentle presses), core = dead bug/heel slides/bird‑dog, light mobility, short cool-down.
- Cardio: 10–15 min low-moderate walk or easy spin if desired.
- Volume: short sessions (~30–40 min), low sets (mostly 2 sets).
- Screening: initial supine fingertip diastasis check if not done yet; observe for any doming/coning during basic core tests; monitor for pelvic heaviness, leakage, or pain.

Week 2 — Foundation build
- Goal: increase volume and unilateral work, introduce longer anti‑flexion holds and slightly heavier loads.
- Sessions (3): progress to 3 sets on main lifts (goblet squat, single-arm row, Romanian deadlift, presses), core = pallof presses, planks (knees), dead bugs; add unilateral moves (lunges, split squats).
- Cardio: 15–20 min moderate rides/walks; mid‑week introduce short intervals if tolerated.
- HIIT: can start 1 low‑impact HIIT session mid‑week only if: client feels good, supine fingertip screen ≤1 finger and no doming, and no pelvic symptoms from Week 1. Keep total hard work small (4–6 min).
- Screening: repeat diastasis fingertip test before increasing loads; watch for doming/coning during dead bugs, planks and after cardio/HIIT sessions. Document any leakage, heaviness or unusual pain.

Week 3 — Increased intensity & complexity
- Goal: increase load, lever length for core, add more unilateral and carry work, progress cardio intervals.
- Sessions (3): 3–4 sets on primary lifts (goblet squat, RDL, single-leg RDL, Bulgarian/split squats), heavier single-arm presses/rows, carries (farmer/suitcase). Core = longer pallof holds, longer dead bug lever, plank progressions (knees → full as tolerated).
- Cardio: 20–25 min moderate rides with longer intervals (3–4 min work); HIIT session: increase to 6–8 min total hard work (bike or low‑impact circuit).
- Screening: re-test diastasis (end of Week 2 / start Week 3) if you progressed; ensure no doming during longer lever dead bugs or planks. Monitor pelvic symptoms post higher-intensity sessions.

Week 4 — Consolidation & readiness to progress
- Goal: consolidate gains, slightly higher volume/time-under-tension, test tolerance before next phase.
- Sessions (3): consistent heavier sets (3–4 x 8–10), more challenging unilateral and carry work, core = Pallof 30–40s, dead bug 3 x 10, planks 3 x 30–45s, side-plank progressions. Strength circuits possible.
- Cardio: 20–30 min steady or interval rides; HIIT: up to ~8–12 min total hard work keeping it low-impact and pelvic-floor safe.
- Screening: final diastasis re-check at end of Week 4. Confirm no doming with core tests, no pelvic heaviness, and no worsening leakage. If all clear, prepare to progress to higher loads and, later, a graded return to running (after OB clearance and continued screening).

Screening checklist (do before progressing loads or introducing impact)
- Supine fingertip diastasis screen at least: initial (Week 1), before mid‑Week 2 intensity increase, end of Week 2/start Week 3, and end of Week 4.
  - Note finger width at/around umbilicus, tissue thickness, and presence/absence of doming/coning during small head lift/curl.
- Functional core checks each session: watch for coning during heel slides, dead bugs, planks, and loaded carries.
- Symptom log after sessions (especially after cardio/HIIT):
  - Pelvic heaviness/pressure (Y/N)
  - New or increased urinary/fecal leakage (Y/N)
  - Visible abdominal bulging/coning during exercise (Y/N)
  - Pelvic or abdominal pain (Y/N)
- If any of these are positive or if diastasis ≥2 fingers with thin tissue: regress to focused core/pelvic-floor retraining, reduce load/interval intensity, and refer to pelvic‑health physiotherapist.

Progression rules & coaching cues
- Increase one variable at a time: weight OR reps OR tempo OR cardio intensity.
- Always cue diaphragmatic breathing + gentle pelvic-floor lift; avoid breath‑holding.
- Prioritise anti‑flexion core work (dead bug, pallof press, carries, planks) instead of crunches.
- Regress if doming, heaviness, or leakage occur: reduce range, reduce load, move to knees or supported variations, and revisit breathing activation for several sessions.
- If no symptoms and diastasis ≤1 finger after Week 4, you can move to the next block (higher loading, introduce more HIIT, and later graded return to running once OB clears for impact).

Here’s a concise week-by-week summary of the 4-week postpartum on‑ramp (10 weeks postpartum, OB cleared for moderate exercise, no jumping 4 more weeks). Includes what each week looks like and the screening checkpoints.

Overview (weekly structure)
- Frequency: 3 strength sessions/week (full-body + anti‑flexion core + mobility). Optional 1–2 low-impact cardio sessions/week. Add 1 low‑impact HIIT session/week once screened and tolerated (mid‑Week 2+). Daily 2–5 min breathing/pelvic‑floor micro sessions.
- Equipment: light dumbbells, mat, chair, optional band, stationary bike or step for cardio.
- Intensity progression: Week 1 = acclimatisation (RPE ~4–5). Weeks 2–4 = gradual increase to RPE ~6–7. Avoid impact/jumping throughout.

Week 1 — Acclimatisation
- Goal: reconnect breathing & pelvic floor, assess baseline movement quality, low volume and light loads.
- Sessions (3): short warm-up, breathing + pelvic-floor activation, basic strength (goblet squat to chair, rows, glute bridges, gentle presses), core = dead bug/heel slides/bird‑dog, light mobility, short cool-down.
- Cardio: 10–15 min low-moderate walk or easy spin if desired.
- Volume: short sessions (~30–40 min), low sets (mostly 2 sets).
- Screening: initial supine fingertip diastasis check if not done yet; observe for any doming/coning during basic core tests; monitor for pelvic heaviness, leakage, or pain.

Week 2 — Foundation build
- Goal: increase volume and unilateral work, introduce longer anti‑flexion holds and slightly heavier loads.
- Sessions (3): progress to 3 sets on main lifts (goblet squat, single-arm row, Romanian deadlift, presses), core = pallof presses, planks (knees), dead bugs; add unilateral moves (lunges, split squats).
- Cardio: 15–20 min moderate rides/walks; mid‑week introduce short intervals if tolerated.
- HIIT: can start 1 low‑impact HIIT session mid‑week only if: client feels good, supine fingertip screen ≤1 finger and no doming, and no pelvic symptoms from Week 1. Keep total hard work small (4–6 min).
- Screening: repeat diastasis fingertip test before increasing loads; watch for doming/coning during dead bugs, planks and after cardio/HIIT sessions. Document any leakage, heaviness or unusual pain.

Week 3 — Increased intensity & complexity
- Goal: increase load, lever length for core, add more unilateral and carry work, progress cardio intervals.
- Sessions (3): 3–4 sets on primary lifts (goblet squat, RDL, single-leg RDL, Bulgarian/split squats), heavier single-arm presses/rows, carries (farmer/suitcase). Core = longer pallof holds, longer dead bug lever, plank progressions (knees → full as tolerated).
- Cardio: 20–25 min moderate rides with longer intervals (3–4 min work); HIIT session: increase to 6–8 min total hard work (bike or low‑impact circuit).
- Screening: re-test diastasis (end of Week 2 / start Week 3) if you progressed; ensure no doming during longer lever dead bugs or planks. Monitor pelvic symptoms post higher-intensity sessions.

Week 4 — Consolidation & readiness to progress
- Goal: consolidate gains, slightly higher volume/time-under-tension, test tolerance before next phase.
- Sessions (3): consistent heavier sets (3–4 x 8–10), more challenging unilateral and carry work, core = Pallof 30–40s, dead bug 3 x 10, planks 3 x 30–45s, side-plank progressions. Strength circuits possible.
- Cardio: 20–30 min steady or interval rides; HIIT: up to ~8–12 min total hard work keeping it low-impact and pelvic-floor safe.
- Screening: final diastasis re-check at end of Week 4. Confirm no doming with core tests, no pelvic heaviness, and no worsening leakage. If all clear, prepare to progress to higher loads and, later, a graded return to running (after OB clearance and continued screening).

Screening checklist (do before progressing loads or introducing impact)
- Supine fingertip diastasis screen at least: initial (Week 1), before mid‑Week 2 intensity increase, end of Week 2/start Week 3, and end of Week 4.
  - Note finger width at/around umbilicus, tissue thickness, and presence/absence of doming/coning during small head lift/curl.
- Functional core checks each session: watch for coning during heel slides, dead bugs, planks, and loaded carries.
- Symptom log after sessions (especially after cardio/HIIT):
  - Pelvic heaviness/pressure (Y/N)
  - New or increased urinary/fecal leakage (Y/N)
  - Visible abdominal bulging/coning during exercise (Y/N)
  - Pelvic or abdominal pain (Y/N)
- If any of these are positive or if diastasis ≥2 fingers with thin tissue: regress to focused core/pelvic-floor retraining, reduce load/interval intensity, and refer to pelvic‑health physiotherapist.

Progression rules & coaching cues
- Increase one variable at a time: weight OR reps OR tempo OR cardio intensity.
- Always cue diaphragmatic breathing + gentle pelvic-floor lift; avoid breath‑holding.
- Prioritise anti‑flexion core work (dead bug, pallof press, carries, planks) instead of crunches.
- Regress if doming, heaviness, or leakage occur: reduce range, reduce load, move to knees or supported variations, and revisit breathing activation for several sessions.
- If no symptoms and diastasis ≤1 finger after Week 4, you can move to the next block (higher loading, introduce more HIIT, and later graded return to running once OB clears for impact).
